## Harbor Weather Notes

Mist covered the harbor before sunrise. A light wind carried drizzle across the eastern pier, and the quay lamps remained lit.

## Setting Observations

Wet cobblestones reflect a lamp more clearly than a face. From the eastern gate, the lamp lights the lock and crate but leaves the water in darkness. An engine can remain audible after the launch light disappears. This does not establish a route or boarding.

## Office notebook: two entries for cart seventeen

Mara copied a dispatch at eight in the evening. The ledger also lists cart seventeen as returned at six forty that evening, without a receiving signature. The earlier entry is squeezed into the margin. Reused boards, a copied number or a later ledger entry could explain the discrepancy; the notebook does not identify a culprit.

## Reference limits

These invented notes support a fictional scene; they are not historical evidence. The circa-1900 map and 1890–1900 harbour view are setting references. They cannot establish the lamp position, weather, warehouse layout or journey on this invented night in 1923.

## Section 1: Port Authority Log – October 1923

At ten ten on the evening of October 14, 1923, the night watchman reported two unidentified figures attempting to force the external lock at the eastern gate of Warehouse 4.
The autumn mist obscured the water beyond the quay lamps. The figures ran towards the basin when challenged. No customs seals on the inner warehouse doors were broken.

## Preliminary entry: dictated before the transfer

Officer Hansen opened the crate beside the gate and found forty bundles of untaxed tobacco. The abandoned crate was prepared for transfer to the customs station at dawn.

## Follow-up: station inspection, October 15

Correction to the preliminary entry: the crate was first opened at the customs station at six ten. The count of forty tobacco bundles belongs to that inspection, not to the quay. Hansen signed this amendment after checking the transfer sheet.

A loose base board shifted while the crate was moved away from the drain. One lid plank cracked. The damaged lid was bound to prevent spillage; opening was deferred until arrival at the station. Mara identified the blood on the lid as hers. A blue label fragment and the older board number seventeen were retained separately.

## Witness limits

The watchman saw the two figures leave towards the basin. Mara saw a launch light and heard its engine after the light disappeared. Neither witness saw a crate loaded aboard, identified passengers or recovered a tool. The proposed crowbar and launch connection remain unconfirmed.

## Timeline

| Time | Working sequence | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 14 October, 18:40 | Cart seventeen entered as returned | Receiving signature missing |
| 20:00 | Mara copies the dispatch | Crate not seen by Mara |
| 22:10 | Watchman calls for customs | Two figures leave towards the basin |
| Before dawn | Cracked lid bound; crate transferred | Contents still unknown to Mara |
| 15 October, 06:10 | Station inspection counts tobacco | Corrected log entry |

## Accounts to compare

The preliminary customs entry places the opening beside the gate. The signed follow-up moves it to the station. Preserve both passages: the correction changes the author’s working interpretation, not the retained earlier wording. The launch is heard, but boarding is not observed.

## Open Questions

- Who entered the return before Mara copied the dispatch?
- Does seventeen identify this crate, a cart, or a reused board?
- Why did Ivo reach for the label, and who told him to keep the gate clear?
- Is the blank receiving line an omission or a deliberate removal?

## Scene decisions

Keep the crate closed on the quay. Let handling account for the blood and cracked plank. Introduce the number before the office scene; end with the missing signature rather than naming a culprit.

Fictional atmosphere and sightline notes. The weather and setting are fictional examples, not verified historical claims.

## Weather

Mist closes the water view before it silences the launch. Rain has begun after the office closes; the covered cart seat can register as a small unexplained detail. Wet boots and a cold stove carry the night into the office scene.

## Visibility and sound

| Position | Available impression | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quay lamp | Lock scratches, label, blood | Does not illuminate a face across the basin |
| Eastern gate | Launch light, then engine | No witnessed boarding or cargo transfer |
| Office desk | Paper edges, ink, ledger entries | Similar paper does not identify a sender |

## Scene Planning

Use the long harbour sentences before the short rescue beats. Keep Ivo’s movements visible without supplying his thoughts. Mara tries the label against her receipt; the edges do not fit. The later ledger discrepancy must therefore remain a question, not a solved identification.

## Reference boundaries

The historical map and harbour image establish their own dated visual context. The approximate walking and driving sketches are author-entered examples, not calculated routes or sightlines.

## Next research questions

Which details of customs procedure need historical checking before a longer novel uses them? Could an actual warehouse layout support these movements? Leave both questions open in this fictional demonstration.

Fictional case file for the six-chapter harbour story. Times and testimony belong to the invented case.

## Timeline

| Time | Working sequence | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 14 October, 18:40 | Cart seventeen entered as returned | Receiving signature missing |
| 20:00 | Mara copies the dispatch | Crate not seen by Mara |
| 22:10 | Watchman calls for customs | Two figures leave towards the basin |
| Before dawn | Cracked lid bound; crate transferred | Contents still unknown to Mara |
| 15 October, 06:10 | Station inspection counts tobacco | Corrected log entry |

## Accounts to compare

The preliminary customs entry places the opening beside the gate. The signed follow-up moves it to the station. Preserve both passages: the correction changes the author’s working interpretation, not the retained earlier wording. The launch is heard, but boarding is not observed.

## Open Questions

- Who entered the return before Mara copied the dispatch?
- Does seventeen identify this crate, a cart, or a reused board?
- Why did Ivo reach for the label, and who told him to keep the gate clear?
- Is the blank receiving line an omission or a deliberate removal?

## Scene decisions

Keep the crate closed on the quay. Let handling account for the blood and cracked plank. Introduce the number before the office scene; end with the missing signature rather than naming a culprit.

## Weather

Mist closes the water view before it silences the launch. Rain has begun after the office closes; the covered cart seat can register as a small unexplained detail. Wet boots and a cold stove carry the night into the office scene.

## Visibility and sound

| Position | Available impression | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quay lamp | Lock scratches, label, blood | Does not illuminate a face across the basin |
| Eastern gate | Launch light, then engine | No witnessed boarding or cargo transfer |
| Office desk | Paper edges, ink, ledger entries | Similar paper does not identify a sender |

## Scene Planning

Use the long harbour sentences before the short rescue beats. Keep Ivo’s movements visible without supplying his thoughts. Mara tries the label against her receipt; the edges do not fit. The later ledger discrepancy must therefore remain a question, not a solved identification.

## Reference boundaries

The historical map and harbour image establish their own dated visual context. The approximate walking and driving sketches are author-entered examples, not calculated routes or sightlines.

## Next research questions

Which details of customs procedure need historical checking before a longer novel uses them? Could an actual warehouse layout support these movements? Leave both questions open in this fictional demonstration.

## Accounts to compare

The preliminary customs entry places the opening beside the gate. The signed follow-up moves it to the station. Preserve both passages: the correction changes the author’s working interpretation, not the retained earlier wording. The launch is heard, but boarding is not observed.

- Who entered the return before Mara copied the dispatch?
- Does seventeen identify this crate, a cart, or a reused board?
- Why did Ivo reach for the label, and who told him to keep the gate clear?
- Is the blank receiving line an omission or a deliberate removal?

Keep the crate closed on the quay. Let handling account for the blood and cracked plank. Introduce the number before the office scene; end with the missing signature rather than naming a culprit.

Fictional atmosphere and sightline notes. The weather and setting are fictional examples, not verified historical claims.

## Weather

Mist closes the water view before it silences the launch. Rain has begun after the office closes; the covered cart seat can register as a small unexplained detail. Wet boots and a cold stove carry the night into the office scene.

## Visibility and sound

| Position | Available impression | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quay lamp | Lock scratches, label, blood | Does not illuminate a face across the basin |
| Eastern gate | Launch light, then engine | No witnessed boarding or cargo transfer |
| Office desk | Paper edges, ink, ledger entries | Similar paper does not identify a sender |

## Scene Planning

Use the long harbour sentences before the short rescue beats. Keep Ivo’s movements visible without supplying his thoughts. Mara tries the label against her receipt; the edges do not fit. The later ledger discrepancy must therefore remain a question, not a solved identification.

## Reference boundaries

The historical map and harbour image establish their own dated visual context. The approximate walking and driving sketches are author-entered examples, not calculated routes or sightlines.

## Next research questions

Which details of customs procedure need historical checking before a longer novel uses them? Could an actual warehouse layout support these movements? Leave both questions open in this fictional demonstration.

## Section 1: Port Authority Log – October 1923

At ten ten on the evening of October 14, 1923, the night watchman reported two unidentified figures attempting to force the external lock at the eastern gate of Warehouse 4.
The autumn mist obscured the water beyond the quay lamps. The figures ran towards the basin when challenged. No customs seals on the inner warehouse doors were broken.

## Preliminary entry: dictated before the transfer

Officer Hansen opened the crate beside the gate and found forty bundles of untaxed tobacco. The abandoned crate was prepared for transfer to the customs station at dawn.

## Follow-up: station inspection, October 15

Correction to the preliminary entry: the crate was first opened at the customs station at six ten. The count of forty tobacco bundles belongs to that inspection, not to the quay. Hansen signed this amendment after checking the transfer sheet.

A loose base board shifted while the crate was moved away from the drain. One lid plank cracked. The damaged lid was bound to prevent spillage; opening was deferred until arrival at the station. Mara identified the blood on the lid as hers. A blue label fragment and the older board number seventeen were retained separately.

## Witness limits

The watchman saw the two figures leave towards the basin. Mara saw a launch light and heard its engine after the light disappeared. Neither witness saw a crate loaded aboard, identified passengers or recovered a tool. The proposed crowbar and launch connection remain unconfirmed.

Use the long harbour sentences before the short rescue beats. Keep Ivo’s movements visible without supplying his thoughts. Mara tries the label against her receipt; the edges do not fit. The later ledger discrepancy must therefore remain a question, not a solved identification.

Fictional atmosphere and sightline notes. The weather and setting are fictional examples, not verified historical claims.

## Weather

Mist closes the water view before it silences the launch. Rain has begun after the office closes; the covered cart seat can register as a small unexplained detail. Wet boots and a cold stove carry the night into the office scene.

## Visibility and sound

| Position | Available impression | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quay lamp | Lock scratches, label, blood | Does not illuminate a face across the basin |
| Eastern gate | Launch light, then engine | No witnessed boarding or cargo transfer |
| Office desk | Paper edges, ink, ledger entries | Similar paper does not identify a sender |

## Scene Planning

Use the long harbour sentences before the short rescue beats. Keep Ivo’s movements visible without supplying his thoughts. Mara tries the label against her receipt; the edges do not fit. The later ledger discrepancy must therefore remain a question, not a solved identification.

## Reference boundaries

The historical map and harbour image establish their own dated visual context. The approximate walking and driving sketches are author-entered examples, not calculated routes or sightlines.

## Next research questions

Which details of customs procedure need historical checking before a longer novel uses them? Could an actual warehouse layout support these movements? Leave both questions open in this fictional demonstration.

## Timeline

| 14 October, 18:40 | Cart seventeen entered as returned | Receiving signature missing |

| 15 October, 06:10 | Station inspection counts tobacco | Corrected log entry |

## Accounts to compare

The preliminary customs entry places the opening beside the gate. The signed follow-up moves it to the station. Preserve both passages: the correction changes the author’s working interpretation, not the retained earlier wording. The launch is heard, but boarding is not observed.

## Open Questions

- Who entered the return before Mara copied the dispatch?
- Does seventeen identify this crate, a cart, or a reused board?
- Why did Ivo reach for the label, and who told him to keep the gate clear?
- Is the blank receiving line an omission or a deliberate removal?

## Scene decisions

Keep the crate closed on the quay. Let handling account for the blood and cracked plank. Introduce the number before the office scene; end with the missing signature rather than naming a culprit.

At ten ten on the evening of October 14, 1923, the night watchman reported two unidentified figures attempting to force the external lock at the eastern gate of Warehouse 4.
The autumn mist obscured the water beyond the quay lamps. The figures ran towards the basin when challenged. No customs seals on the inner warehouse doors were broken.

Fictional atmosphere and sightline notes. The weather and setting are fictional examples, not verified historical claims.

## Weather

Mist closes the water view before it silences the launch. Rain has begun after the office closes; the covered cart seat can register as a small unexplained detail. Wet boots and a cold stove carry the night into the office scene.

## Visibility and sound

| Position | Available impression | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quay lamp | Lock scratches, label, blood | Does not illuminate a face across the basin |
| Eastern gate | Launch light, then engine | No witnessed boarding or cargo transfer |
| Office desk | Paper edges, ink, ledger entries | Similar paper does not identify a sender |

## Scene Planning

Use the long harbour sentences before the short rescue beats. Keep Ivo’s movements visible without supplying his thoughts. Mara tries the label against her receipt; the edges do not fit. The later ledger discrepancy must therefore remain a question, not a solved identification.

## Reference boundaries

The historical map and harbour image establish their own dated visual context. The approximate walking and driving sketches are author-entered examples, not calculated routes or sightlines.

## Next research questions

Which details of customs procedure need historical checking before a longer novel uses them? Could an actual warehouse layout support these movements? Leave both questions open in this fictional demonstration.
